analysis.one_liner: Legislatively approves the Keystone XL pipeline permit and ends further federal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced with 75 cosponsors in January 2012, it was referred to three committees and a subcommittee and died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have used an Act of Congress to grant the federal permit for the Keystone XL pipeline, which normally requires presidential approval after a State Department review. It declared that the environmental impact statement already issued satisfied all environmental law requirements and that no further federal environmental review would be needed. It also required the president to approve whatever route through Nebraska the state's governor submitted, with the route automatically approved if the president did not act within 10 days.
analysis.who_benefits: TransCanada, the company behind the pipeline, and Canadian oil sands producers would get a congressionally guaranteed permit without further environmental review. Gulf Coast refiners would gain a new supply of heavy Canadian crude, and supporters pointed to pipeline construction jobs and reduced reliance on overseas oil.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that the permit for the Keystone XL pipeline project 'is hereby approved,' turning a pending executive-branch permit decision into law [S3].

It declares that the State Department's final environmental impact statement of August 26, 2011 satisfies the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act, and that 'no further Federal environmental review shall be required' [S3].

It keeps in place the construction, mitigation, and reclamation measures and pipeline safety special conditions agreed to in the environmental review, including specific Sand Hills protections if the route crosses that region [S3].
It mandates a Nebraska routing reconsideration, and deems the governor-submitted route approved 'by operation of law' if the president does not act within 10 days [S3].

The bill includes a savings clause stating that it does not alter the processes needed to secure access from private property owners, leaving existing eminent domain and access procedures untouched [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities and landowners along the pipeline route, particularly in Nebraska's Sand Hills and over the Ogallala aquifer, would bear the risk of a project approved with the federal environmental review process cut short. The broader public would lose the chance to have one specific project's environmental impacts examined further before construction. The political cost is precedent: Congress would be handing a permit to a single named company's project, bypassing the executive review that applies to every other border-crossing pipeline.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nebraska landowners and communities along the route

drawbacks.text: The bill eliminates further federal environmental review for this one project by declaring the existing environmental impact statement legally sufficient and barring any additional review, regardless of route changes [S3].
It strips the president of real discretion over the Nebraska route: the governor's submitted route must be approved within 10 days or it becomes approved automatically by law [S3].

The strongest good-faith objection is that this is legislation for a single company's permit — Congress would be doing the State Department's job for one project, a precedent that could be applied to any future disputed pipeline.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill's speed comes at the expense of the routing review Nebraska politicians were demanding; the bill fast-tracks that review but removes the public's leverage to slow or stop the project if concerns emerged.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered a guaranteed permit quickly to one company, with construction safety conditions and Nebraska Sand Hills protections preserved from the existing review. But its core trade is deliberate: guaranteed speed for the pipeline in exchange for shutting down further environmental scrutiny of a project crossing a major aquifer region. For anyone who valued the environmental review process, the bargain was poor; for the pipeline's sponsors, it was everything they wanted.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees and a pipelines subcommittee in its first week, and none of them ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Poe introduced the bill on January 24, 2012, with the permit 'hereby approved' in the bill's text [S3], [S5].

The same day, it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure, Energy and Commerce, and Natural Resources committees, and on January 25 to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials [S5].

The only recorded action after referral was the sponsor's introductory remarks on January 31, 2012; no committee marked it up, no floor vote ever occurred, and the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].
The bill attracted 75 cosponsors — 74 Republicans and 1 Democrat — none of which was enough to move it out of committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died quietly in committee, the Keystone XL permit stayed in the executive branch and the full environmental review process remained in place for anyone on that path; nobody's situation changed directly, but the pipeline's sponsors failed to get the legislative shortcut they sought.

for.name: Rep. Ted Poe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill legislatively approving the Keystone XL permit and made introductory remarks on the House floor [S3], [S5].

for.name: Rep. Dan Boren
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, the bill's sole Democratic cosponsor [S3], [S4].

against.name: John Mica
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee (112th Congress)
against.what_they_did: The committee, to which the bill was first referred, never reported it out or scheduled a markup; the record shows no committee action after referral [S5].

against.name: President Barack Obama
against.what_they_did: Denied the State Department permit for the Keystone XL pipeline in January 2012, the decision this bill would have overridden by statute, and opposed congressional attempts to approve the project.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 74 of the 75 cosponsors were Republicans, with a single Democrat, Rep. Dan Boren of Oklahoma, joining [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have granted its pending federal permit by statute, with no further federal environmental review and an automatic Nebraska route approval after 10 days [S3]. Its gain came from ending the review process ordinary people rely on to scrutinize a pipeline crossing sensitive water and land.

A guaranteed pipeline would lock in a route to U.S. Gulf Coast markets for heavy Alberta crude, a commercial benefit with no direct offsetting cost or benefit to consumers; any consumer effect would depend on oil markets.
The pipeline would supply Gulf refineries with heavy Canadian crude, supporting their feedstock position; the effect on consumer fuel prices was disputed and not resolved by the record.
Construction of the pipeline means construction jobs, the main benefit supporters cited for workers along the route.

industries.industry: Nebraska landowners and agricultural communities over the Ogallala aquifer and Sand Hills
industries.note: The bill cut off further federal environmental review of the route over a major aquifer and through the Sand Hills, while keeping existing property-access processes intact [S3]. Landowners would bear construction disruption and spill risk with less environmental scrutiny.
